lesson_title: The Cypherpunk Ethos and Decentralized Trust

questions.question_stem: A user wants online payments that can be reversed after fraud, but also wants no institution to be able to block lawful transactions. Which tradeoff does this scenario illustrate?
questions.correct_answer: Centralized intermediaries can provide verification and reversibility, but they also create censorship points and single points of failure.
incorrect_answers: Decentralized payment systems can reduce bank reliance while preserving the same chargeback protections without any censorable operator.
Cryptographic signatures can make payments private and reversible while keeping transaction approval outside institutional control.
Peer-to-peer settlement can remove fraud risk by letting users coordinate directly, so reversibility and censorship resistance stop conflicting.
questions.explanation: The lesson frames centralized trust as useful for verification, recordkeeping, and reversibility, while also introducing fees, control points, and high-value targets.

questions.question_stem: Within the cypherpunk ethos, why is privacy treated as something to build into systems rather than request from institutions?
questions.correct_answer: Because privacy depends on default technical architecture, not only on institutional promises about how data will be handled.
incorrect_answers: Because privacy is mainly created by after-the-fact legal limits on how centralized databases may share collected records.
Because encrypting message contents by itself prevents institutions from collecting metadata, routing records, or identity data.
Because publishing code matters less than certifying a trusted operator who can enforce anonymity for all users online.
questions.explanation: The lesson emphasizes privacy by default through code and selective disclosure, rather than reliance on governments or corporations to grant privacy after the fact.

questions.question_stem: Why did the Crypto Wars matter to the historical foundation of blockchain?
questions.correct_answer: They showed the conflict over public access to strong cryptography and helped establish code as a tool for resisting centralized control.
incorrect_answers: They showed that early digital cash failed mainly from weak peer-to-peer markets and helped establish mining as a way to issue currency.
They demonstrated that licensed financial networks could protect private records and helped establish banks as the source of online privacy.
They showed that privacy disputes were resolved through financial regulation and helped establish law as the main defense for private communication.
questions.explanation: The Crypto Wars support the lesson's theme that public cryptography and code distribution were part of the political and technical foundation for later decentralized systems.

questions.question_stem: An early digital cash service uses strong privacy-preserving cryptography but depends on one company and its banking relationships. What is the main unresolved weakness?
questions.correct_answer: The service can still collapse or be shut down because its organization and partners are centralized points of failure.
incorrect_answers: The service remains weak because blind-signature privacy stops the operator from checking whether the same coin was spent twice.
The service remains weak because public-key cryptography forces each payer to reveal a legal identity to every other user.
The service remains weak because peer-to-peer routing, rather than corporate dependency, becomes the primary shutdown target.
questions.explanation: The lesson distinguishes cryptographic strength from architectural resilience: earlier systems could protect some transaction details yet remain vulnerable through central companies, servers, or banking partners.

questions.question_stem: A file-sharing network has many users exchanging files directly, but everyone must first query one central directory server. How should its resilience be classified?
questions.correct_answer: It is only partially decentralized because the central directory remains a legal and technical takedown target.
incorrect_answers: It is fully decentralized because actual file transfers happen directly between users instead of through the directory.
It is centrally routed because each file transfer must pass through the directory server before reaching another user.
It is resilient like a distributed hash table because file indexes are shared across users after the first search.
questions.explanation: The lesson uses hybrid P2P designs to show that a central index can preserve a single point of control even when user-to-user exchange is decentralized.

questions.question_stem: Which description best captures Bitcoin's originality?
questions.correct_answer: Bitcoin combined existing cryptography, cypherpunk goals, peer-to-peer networking, past digital-cash lessons, and proof-of-work to solve decentralized agreement over transaction history.
incorrect_answers: Bitcoin made earlier electronic-cash ideas work by adding a central reserve operator that could settle transactions while publishing open-source cryptography and auditing bank partners.
Bitcoin created anonymous online payments by hiding all ledger data, replacing public verification with encrypted balances held by users, and keeping transaction histories off-chain.
Bitcoin mainly improved existing payment networks by lowering merchant fees while leaving consensus, identity checks, and currency issuance to financial institutions in practice.
questions.explanation: The lesson presents Bitcoin as a combination of prior technical and ideological ingredients, with proof-of-work enabling leaderless consensus against double-spending.

questions.question_stem: What specific problem does proof-of-work help solve for a decentralized digital money network?
questions.correct_answer: It helps a leaderless network converge on one transaction history, making double-spending difficult without a trusted intermediary.
incorrect_answers: It assigns each transaction to a known validator identity, making fraud disputes reversible through account recovery services.
It encrypts transaction details before broadcast, making the public ledger private even though peers still relay blocks across the network.
It distributes wallet keys across many nodes, making stolen credentials unusable without separate approval from the network.
questions.explanation: Proof-of-work is presented as the mechanism that lets strangers coordinate on a shared history without a central leader, addressing double-spending in an open P2P environment.

questions.question_stem: A student says, "Bitcoin has no names on-chain, so it is completely anonymous." What is the best correction?
questions.correct_answer: Bitcoin is pseudonymous: activity is tied to identifiers on a public ledger, and those identifiers can sometimes be linked to real people.
incorrect_answers: Bitcoin is encrypted: transaction contents are hidden on-chain, so outside observers need private keys to read payment histories.
Bitcoin is anonymous: addresses are not names, so repeated activity stays separate across transactions and later exchange records by default.
Bitcoin is private like a bank account: custodians know identities, while public users cannot inspect transaction history directly.
questions.explanation: The lesson separates pseudonymity from anonymity. Public blockchain records can support tracing even when real-world names are not directly written into transactions.

questions.question_stem: A user buys cryptocurrency through an exchange, leaves funds in an exchange account, and relies on the exchange for recovery support. What does this show about the "promise versus reality" of decentralization?
questions.correct_answer: Even if the base protocol reduces intermediaries, the surrounding ecosystem can reintroduce centralized trust relationships.
incorrect_answers: Even if a public ledger is decentralized, it supplies customer support and recovery, so exchanges are only display interfaces.
Even if proof-of-work secures settlement, the network can reverse exchange mistakes without a custody intermediary.
Even if users choose custodial services, decentralization has failed at the protocol layer rather than at the access layer.
questions.explanation: The lesson notes that blockchains did not eliminate all intermediaries; exchanges and wallet providers can become new points of custody, control, and reliance.

questions.question_stem: Why do decentralized systems require a different threat model from traditional online banking systems?
questions.correct_answer: Attackers may target consensus rules, majority control, and incentives rather than only a central database or server perimeter.
incorrect_answers: Attackers mainly focus on branch offices, payment processors, and customer support workflows rather than protocol-level incentives.
Defenders can assume there is no central server to protect, so decentralized systems no longer need operational security.
The main risk shifts to ordinary banking compliance because decentralized nodes all operate under one administrator.
questions.explanation: Decentralization can reduce some single-server risks, but it creates protocol-level and economic attack surfaces such as consensus manipulation.

questions.question_stem: In Hughes's argument, what distinguishes privacy from secrecy?
questions.correct_answer: Privacy is selective disclosure: revealing identity or information when appropriate, rather than hiding everything from everyone.
incorrect_answers: Privacy means hiding communications from the public, while secrecy means proving identity to a trusted party whenever challenged online.
Privacy means encrypting message content for confidentiality, while secrecy means using signatures to reveal identity to everyone by default.
Privacy means institutions promise not to share collected records, while secrecy means users deploy code without prior legal approval.
questions.explanation: The reading defines privacy as control over what is revealed and when, which allows voluntary identity disclosure instead of total concealment.

questions.question_stem: Which online transaction design best follows the data-minimization principle?
questions.correct_answer: The system reveals only the information needed to complete the transaction, while avoiding unnecessary identity and relationship data exposure.
incorrect_answers: The system verifies full legal identity at account creation, then uses encryption to hide message contents from outside observers.
The system stores detailed histories and social graph metadata, then limits staff access through company policies and audit logs.
The system publishes transaction identifiers for transparency, then tells users to avoid linking those records to real-world names.
questions.explanation: Hughes argues that electronic transactions should disclose only what the transaction requires because aggregation of extra information undermines privacy.
questions.lesson_block: Reading: Transaction Design And Data Minimization

questions.question_stem: According to Hughes, why can digital signatures fit within a privacy-preserving system rather than contradict it?
questions.correct_answer: They allow assured identity disclosure when a user chooses to authenticate, while default transactions can still minimize identity exposure.
incorrect_answers: They make each transaction anonymous by encrypting both sender identity and message content under one public signature scheme for users.
They require users to identify themselves to a central operator before anonymous transactions can be accepted by the payment network.
They replace selective disclosure with permanent identity binding, so privacy-preserving systems use them only for regulatory reporting.
questions.explanation: The reading pairs anonymous transaction systems with digital signatures: privacy can include chosen authentication rather than constant identity exposure.
